Now coming to Indian agriculture and agrochemical industry. How did the industry perform 
over the last 6 months of the current financial year. H1 FY '27 was one of the most difficult first 
halves for the Indian agrochemical industry in over a decade. The main reason was the erratic 
and unpredictable monsoon. The Southwest monsoon arrived late and started weak. 
June rainfall was about 35% below normal. Generally, June month rainfall is very critical for 
the sowing operations by the farmers. Because of the delayed rainfall, the sowing of the key 
crops were delayed until mid-July. July rainfall was close to normal. Of course it did not cover 
the shortfall of the June rainfall.  
August was dry again, about 16% below the normal rainfall and September did not make up this 
shortfall. Overall, the season ended with a deficit of almost 13% of the normal rainfall. As per 
the IMD, this was the fourth weakest monsoon since 2001 and the weakest since 2015. Rainfall 
was very uneven.  
East and Northeast India had their lowest monsoon rainfall since 1901 and the South Peninsula 
was about 24% below normal. Of the 23 key agricultural states, 16 had deficit rainfall of more 
than 10%; some even went up to 30% - 40%. Several states, including Maharashtra, Karnataka, 
Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan have declared drought in large parts of the area.  
Furthermore, India as a country, IMD has declared it as officially a drought year. Farmers were 
able to complete sowing with whatever water that was made available, was available by the 
monsoon and kharif acreage ended little bit lower than normal, about 1.5% below normal. Rice 
was the main exception with the acreage almost lower by 4%. 
However, there were very few days of above normal rainfall during the season and crops faced 
long dry spells at the stage when they needed their inputs most, which impacted the agrochemical 
consumption. Delayed sowing and dry spells reduced herbicide consumption. In August and 
September, farmers skipped spray rounds, which lowered demand for insecticides and 
fungicides.  
Industry reports also show that farmers cut back on total overall agricultural inputs. Production 
of key crops such as rice, cotton, soybean, groundnut, pulses and oilseeds is now estimated to 
be lower than by almost 10% depending on the crop. To begin at the beginning of the year 
between March and May. 
The cost increased because of the Middle Eastern war, the technical prices went up, a weaker 
rupee depreciation and high packaging, solvent and freight costs added to the overall cost of 
inputs. Companies including SCIL passed on these increases to a large extent. However, because 
of the erratic monsoon sensing that the season was not going to be normal, from June onwards, 
the prices started falling.  
Some companies took the price correction. Some companies decided to maintain the price. The 
industry, therefore, carried high cost inventory into the period of lower volume and softer prices 
in Q2. SCIL team focused on key products which were critical for our success. Those products 
performed very well.

Third, the Northeast monsoon began on 15th of October. It has rained well in a couple of areas 
in Southern geography.

moisture conditions compared to normal period. There are also some positives. Lower harvest

All the commodity prices are going up, which means that the farmers are getting the benefit in 
terms of income, which would put them in a position to invest in their second crop, in crop 
protection apart from other agri inputs. Where crop area holds up and prices remain firm, we 
expect consumption to be broadly normal.
